Newborn Care

Newborn Fever: Why 100.4 F Means Call Right Away

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A rectal temperature of 100.4 F (38.0 C) or higher in a baby under 3 months old is a fever, and it means calling a clinician right away, even at night, so your baby is evaluated the same day. In a baby under 28 days, treat it as an emergency and seek care right away. Young infants can have serious infections with almost no other signs, so the number alone is the reason to call. This guide covers how to measure accurately, what to do next, and why unusually low readings matter too.

Why 100.4 F is the line for young babies

For a baby under 3 months old, a rectal temperature of 100.4 F (38.0 C) or higher is a fever, and at this age it is never something to watch and wait on. Pediatric guidance, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, advises that these babies be evaluated by a clinician the same day, and a baby under 28 days should be seen urgently, usually in an emergency department. This is true even if your baby is feeding, sleeping, and acting normally. The number itself is the signal. You are not overreacting by calling at 2 a.m., and no reasonable clinician will think you are.

The reason for the strict cutoff is how young immune systems work. In the first weeks of life, a baby's defenses are still immature, and bacteria can spread quickly through the blood, urine, or spinal fluid without producing the obvious signs an older child would show. A newborn with a serious infection may look only slightly off, or may look fine. Fever is sometimes the single clue, which is why clinicians take one reading so seriously. Once a baby is past 3 months, the rules relax and behavior starts to matter more than the number. Before then, the threshold does the deciding for you.

How to take your newborn's temperature

A rectal reading with a digital thermometer is the standard at this age because it reflects core temperature most accurately. Wash the thermometer tip with soap and cool water, then coat it with a little petroleum jelly or a water-based lubricant. Lay your baby on their back and lift the legs gently toward the chest, or place them belly down across your lap. Insert the tip about half an inch, no more than one inch, and stop if you feel resistance. Hold it still until it beeps, then read the number and write it down with the time. Label that thermometer rectal only so it never gets used for mouths.

Forehead and armpit thermometers are useful for screening, but they can read high or low, so they should not make the final call at this age. If a forehead or armpit reading looks raised, or your baby simply feels hot to you, confirm with a rectal measurement before deciding anything. If you cannot take a rectal reading, call the clinician anyway and say which method you used. Ear thermometers are not reliable in young babies because the ear canal is too small. Do not add or subtract a degree to convert one method to another; just take a rectal reading. And skip the wrist-on-forehead test as your only check. Hands are good at noticing warmth and bad at measuring it.

What to do when the number is 100.4 F or higher

Call your baby's clinician or nurse line right away, whatever the hour. If your baby is under 28 days old, go to an emergency department; most clinicians will send you there anyway, because babies this young usually need tests such as urine and blood work to rule out serious infection. If your baby is between 28 days and 3 months, the clinician will tell you whether to come to the office quickly or go straight to emergency care. Do not wait to see whether the fever comes down on its own, and do not wait for morning. A fever that fades for a few hours can still mean infection.

Before you leave, or while you wait for a callback, note the exact reading, the time, and how you measured it, in the BeMama app or on paper. If you took more than one reading, note them all. This small record genuinely helps, because the care team will ask when the fever started and how high it went. Dress your baby in a normal single layer for the trip, not extra bundling. Bring the thermometer if it is easy to grab. Feeding can continue as usual unless a clinician says otherwise. Your only jobs right now are to get seen and to keep the timeline straight.

What not to do before your baby is seen

Do not give acetaminophen (Tylenol) or ibuprofen unless a clinician specifically directs it. Fever medicine is not dangerous in the right dose, but at this age the dose must come from a professional, and lowering the number before evaluation hides the very information the team needs. Ibuprofen is not used in babies under about 6 months at all. If a clinician does recommend acetaminophen, they will give you a dose based on your baby's weight; never guess from the package, which does not cover young infants. A fever brought down at home is still a fever that happened, and it still needs the same evaluation.

Do not assume warm clothing explains the reading without proving it. If your baby was heavily bundled or in a hot room, undress them to a single light layer, wait about 15 to 30 minutes, and take another rectal reading. If it is still 100.4 F or higher, call. If it has dropped below the line, keep the room comfortable, recheck later, and call anyway if anything about your baby worries you. Skip cold baths, cool sponging, and rubbing alcohol; they can cause shivering or harm and do not treat the cause. Rechecking every ten minutes all night is not a plan either. One confirmed reading is enough to act on.

A low temperature needs a call too

Fever is not the only reading that matters in a newborn. A rectal temperature below about 97.5 F (36.4 C) also deserves a prompt call to your baby's clinician. Young babies lose heat quickly and are not yet good at holding a steady temperature, so a low number sometimes just means a cool room or damp clothes. But in newborns, a low temperature can also be a sign of infection, in the same way a fever can. Clinicians treat an unusually low reading in a young infant with the same seriousness as a high one, which is why it earns a call rather than a shrug.

If the reading is low, warm your baby the simple way: dry clothes, a hat, skin to skin contact against your chest with a blanket over both of you, and a comfortably warm room. Recheck after about 30 minutes. If the temperature stays below 97.5 F despite warming, or your baby is hard to wake or feeding poorly, seek medical care promptly rather than continuing to warm and wait. Avoid hot water bottles, heating pads, and space heaters aimed at the crib; they can overheat or burn a newborn quickly. As with fever, you are not measuring to reassure yourself. You are measuring to know when to call.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

A rectal temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher in a baby three months or younger requires immediate medical contact, even when the baby otherwise appears well. Young infants can have serious infection without many obvious symptoms.

Breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, marked sleepiness, seizures, persistent vomiting, dehydration, poor feeding, or a rapidly changing rash also require urgent assessment.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to record the exact temperature, method, time, feeding, diapers, and symptoms while arranging care. Do not wait for a trend or AI response before calling.

When to seek help

Call the baby’s clinician or urgent service immediately for fever in a young infant; use emergency services for severe breathing, responsiveness, colour, or seizure concerns.

Sources and further reading

  • American Academy of Pediatrics — Fever and Your Baby

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • A rectal temperature of 100.4 F (38.0 C) or higher in a baby under 3 months needs same day medical care.
  • For a baby under 28 days, go to emergency care right away.
  • Rectal measurement is the standard at this age; forehead and armpit readings are screening only.
  • Do not give fever medicine before evaluation unless a clinician tells you to.
  • A rectal reading below about 97.5 F (36.4 C) also deserves a prompt call.

Frequently asked questions

What temperature is a fever for a newborn?

A rectal temperature of 100.4 F (38.0 C) or higher is a fever in a newborn. In any baby under 3 months, that number means same day medical evaluation, even if your baby seems well. Forehead and armpit readings are screening only, so confirm with a rectal measurement before deciding anything.

Is 100.4 a fever for a baby?

Yes. A rectal reading of 100.4 F (38.0 C) is the fever threshold for babies, and under 3 months it is the level at which clinicians want the baby seen the same day. It is a call now number, not a watch and wait number, because young infants can have serious infections with few other signs.

Can you give Tylenol to a newborn?

Not unless a clinician directs it. Acetaminophen dosing in babies under 12 weeks should come from a professional and be based on your baby's weight, and giving it before an evaluation can hide the fever the care team needs to see. Ibuprofen is not used under about 6 months. Call first; if medicine is appropriate, you will get an exact dose.

When should I take my baby to the ER for a fever?

Go to the emergency department for any rectal temperature of 100.4 F (38.0 C) or higher in a baby under 28 days old. For a baby between 28 days and 3 months, call your clinician immediately; depending on the hour and your baby's history, they may see you urgently or send you to emergency care. If you cannot reach anyone, go to the ER rather than waiting.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
